title: The Levant's Ottoman Collapse
subtitle: 1908–1920 AD · The Young Turk Era, the Arab Revolt, and Contradictory Wartime Promises

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Revolution, world war, an Arab revolt, and a kingdom crushed at Maysalun

entries.label: The Young Turk Revolution
entries.hint: A military-led uprising by the Committee of Union and Progress forced Sultan Abdul Hamid II to restore the suspended 1876 constitution and reconvene parliament, a moment many Arab intellectuals and notables initially welcomed as promising genuine constitutional equality — an optimism that soured over the following years as the CUP's dominant faction increasingly pursued Turkish-centred centralising policies many Arab provincial elites experienced as a new kind of marginalisation rather than the equal partnership the revolution had seemed to promise.
entries.note: Compare ottoman-syria-1800-1908::p5 for Abdul Hamid II's preceding autocratic period, which the 1908 revolution directly ended.

entries.label: Ottoman Entry into World War I
entries.hint: The Ottoman Empire's alliance with Germany and Austria-Hungary drew Syria and Palestine directly into a world war for the first time, subjecting the region to conscription, requisitioning and, as covered in the Economy entry below, catastrophic wartime famine conditions well before any Allied military campaign reached its own territory.
entries.note: Ottoman Empire's entry into World War I, October–November 1914.

entries.label: The Arab Revolt Begins
entries.hint: Sharif Hussein bin Ali of Mecca proclaimed revolt against Ottoman rule, having secured British assurances of support for postwar Arab independence through correspondence with the British High Commissioner in Egypt — assurances whose exact territorial scope, particularly regarding Palestine and the Syrian coast, remained genuinely and consequentially ambiguous, a vagueness that would collide directly with commitments Britain was simultaneously making elsewhere, as the Order entries below describe.
entries.note: The Hussein-McMahon Correspondence, 1915–1916, is covered in full in the Order entry below.
keywords: Sharif Hussein bin Ali of Mecca

entries.label: Allenby's Sinai and Palestine Campaign
entries.hint: General Edmund Allenby's British Egyptian Expeditionary Force, advancing alongside Arab Revolt forces further east, captured Gaza, Jerusalem and ultimately Damascus over roughly eighteen months of campaigning — ending four centuries of continuous Ottoman rule over the Levant and setting the stage for the immediate, contested question of what political arrangements would replace it.
entries.note: Compare the Conflict entries below for the specific battles and captures this campaign involved.
keywords: Edmund Allenby British Egyptian Expeditionary Force

entries.label: Faisal's Arab Kingdom of Syria
entries.hint: Sharif Hussein's son Faisal established an Arab administration in Damascus immediately after the city's capture, convened a Syrian National Congress, and was proclaimed King of Syria in March 1920 — an assertion of Arab self-government that directly contradicted the interior Syrian sphere France had been assigned under the secret 1916 Sykes-Picot Agreement, a collision the following Conflict entry resolves by force rather than negotiation.
entries.note: Faisal's Arab Kingdom of Syria, October 1918 – July 1920; compare mandate-syria-lebanon-1920-1946 for the French Mandate period this kingdom's fall directly opens.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Aqaba, Jerusalem, Damascus, and the battle ending Arab self-rule

entries.label: The Battle of Aqaba
entries.hint: Arab Revolt forces under Faisal, advised by T.E. Lawrence, executed a celebrated overland surprise attack across difficult desert terrain to seize Aqaba from its undefended landward side rather than assaulting its heavily fortified sea approach — a major propaganda and strategic success that opened a supply route supporting the revolt's subsequent push north.
entries.note: T.E. Lawrence's own account in Seven Pillars of Wisdom remains the most widely read narrative of the attack; compare the Thought entry below on reading his memoir with appropriate critical distance.

entries.label: The Capture of Jerusalem
entries.hint: General Allenby's forces took Jerusalem after the Ottoman garrison withdrew without a defensive battle for the city itself, and Allenby deliberately entered on foot through the Jaffa Gate rather than on horseback — a calculated gesture of humility toward the city's religious significance, and one contemporaries and later historians alike noted as a pointed contrast to Kaiser Wilhelm II's triumphant mounted entry two decades earlier in 1898.
entries.note: Allenby's proclamation and ceremonial entry, 11 December 1917; compare the Belief entry below on the entry's deliberate symbolism.

entries.label: The Capture of Damascus
entries.hint: Arab Revolt forces and British and Australian cavalry both entered Damascus within hours of each other on 1 October 1918, a moment of genuine and still-debated ambiguity over which force effectively "liberated" the city first — British and Arab accounts of the day's exact sequence differ in ways that reflect the same underlying tension between Arab self-governance claims and Allied military and political control that would shape the following two years.
entries.note: Contemporary British and Arab accounts of the 1 October 1918 entry into Damascus differ on sequence and emphasis in ways later historians have noted reflect this broader political tension.

entries.label: The Battle of Maysalun
entries.hint: French forces under General Gouraud decisively defeated Faisal's small, poorly equipped army west of Damascus, killing the Syrian minister of war Yusuf al-Azma as he led a doomed last stand — a brief, one-sided battle that ended Faisal's kingdom outright and opened direct French Mandate rule over Syria within days, the clearest possible demonstration that Sykes-Picot's earlier secret division of the region would be enforced by arms rather than negotiated away.
entries.note: Battle of Maysalun, 24 July 1920; compare mandate-syria-lebanon-1920-1946 for the French Mandate period beginning immediately afterward.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Three wartime promises that could not all be kept at once

entries.label: The Hussein-McMahon Correspondence
entries.hint: A series of letters between Sharif Hussein and British High Commissioner Henry McMahon pledged British support for Arab independence across a broadly described territory in exchange for revolt against the Ottomans — the correspondence's own wording left the precise boundaries, especially concerning Palestine and the Syrian coast, genuinely ambiguous, an ambiguity that later became bitterly contested once its tension with Britain's other, secret wartime commitments came to light.
entries.note: Hussein-McMahon Correspondence, July 1915 – March 1916; the disputed territorial scope, particularly regarding Palestine, remains a genuinely unresolved historiographical question rather than a settled matter.

entries.label: The Sykes-Picot Agreement
entries.hint: British diplomat Mark Sykes and French diplomat François Georges-Picot secretly negotiated a division of Ottoman Arab territories into direct-control and influence zones — France receiving coastal Syria and Lebanon directly plus an inland sphere including Damascus and Aleppo, Britain receiving Mesopotamia directly plus a sphere covering Transjordan, and Palestine itself marked for some form of international administration — an agreement in direct tension with the independence Britain had implicitly promised Hussein, whose public exposure by the Bolsheviks in late 1917 caused genuine shock and lasting anger once Arab nationalists learned of its existence.
entries.note: Sykes-Picot Agreement, negotiated May 1916, kept secret until the Bolshevik government published seized Russian diplomatic archives in November 1917.

entries.label: The Balfour Declaration
entries.hint: British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour's letter to the Zionist leader Lord Rothschild stated the government "view[ed] with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people," while adding that nothing should be done to "prejudice the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities in Palestine" — a brief document, issued without consulting Palestine's existing population, that reflected genuine British sympathy toward Zionism among some officials alongside calculated wartime diplomatic considerations, and that added a third, distinct set of commitments to a region where two others already stood in evident tension with each other.
entries.note: Balfour Declaration, 2 November 1917; the document's drafting history, motivations and precise legal weight remain the subject of extensive ongoing historical scholarship and debate, engaged with here only as to its own text and immediate 1917 context.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: A general dismounts before Jerusalem's gates

entries.label: A General Dismounts before Jerusalem's Gates
entries.hint: Allenby's decision to walk rather than ride into Jerusalem, reportedly out of explicit deference to the city's status as sacred to three religions, was a carefully calculated piece of public symbolism in an era when European powers were keenly aware that how they were seen entering the Holy City mattered as much to global and local opinion as the military fact of its capture itself.
entries.note: Contemporary press coverage across Britain, the wider Allied world and locally in Palestine gave Allenby's entry considerable symbolic attention, widely contrasted against Kaiser Wilhelm II's 1898 mounted entry.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: A new documentary medium captures a very old land at war

entries.label: Film and Photography Capture a Land at War
entries.hint: British official cameramen and photographers documented the Palestine campaign in far greater visual detail than any earlier conflict fought over this land, producing newsreel footage and photographs of Allenby's Jerusalem entry, the Arab Revolt forces and the campaign's aftermath that circulated widely in cinemas and newspapers back in Britain — the first time this specific landscape's modern conflicts were captured and consumed by mass audiences as moving images rather than only text and illustration.
entries.note: Imperial War Museum and other archival newsreel and photographic collections document the 1917–1918 Palestine campaign in unprecedented visual detail for the region.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Secret nationalist societies organize, and one soldier's contested memoir

entries.label: Secret Arab Nationalist Societies Organise
entries.hint: Underground organisations like al-Fatat, founded by Arab students in Paris in 1911, and al-Ahd, a network of Arab officers within the Ottoman military, coordinated nationalist political activity well before the Arab Revolt's public outbreak, providing much of the organisational backbone and personnel that would staff Faisal's subsequent Damascus administration — a less romantically documented but arguably more consequential thread of the period than the military campaign itself.
entries.note: al-Fatat (founded Paris, 1911) and al-Ahd, key secret Arab nationalist societies whose membership substantially overlapped with Faisal's later Syrian government personnel.

entries.label: T.E. Lawrence's Contested Legacy as a Source
entries.hint: T.E. Lawrence's own memoir of the revolt, published in various forms through the 1920s, became by far the most widely read Western account of these events and shaped popular understanding of the Arab Revolt for a century afterward — a vivid, genuinely important primary source that modern historians nonetheless read with real caution, since Lawrence's own literary self-presentation is now widely understood to have inflated his personal role relative to the more collaborative and often more mundane realities other British and, especially, Arab participants' own accounts describe.
entries.note: T.E. Lawrence, Seven Pillars of Wisdom, various editions 1922–1926; modern historiography (following, among others, work explicitly centring Arab participants' own perspectives) treats Lawrence's self-presentation with considerably more critical distance than earlier popular accounts did.

entries.label: The Great Famine of Mount Lebanon
entries.hint: An Allied naval blockade intended to pressure the Ottoman war effort, combined with Ottoman military requisitioning of food, animals and labour, a severe locust plague in 1915, and the wartime disruption of normal trade, produced a catastrophic famine across Mount Lebanon that killed a very substantial proportion of its prewar population — estimates vary in the scholarly literature but commonly range around 200,000 deaths, potentially a third or more of the region's population, making it one of the First World War's most severe civilian death tolls anywhere, despite receiving comparatively little attention in general historical memory of the war.
entries.note: Death toll estimates for the 1915–1918 Mount Lebanon famine vary across scholarly sources (commonly cited figures range from roughly 100,000 to over 200,000); causation is generally attributed to the convergence of blockade, requisitioning, locusts and inadequate relief rather than any single factor.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Aircraft bring industrial warfare to the region

entries.label: Aircraft Bring Industrial Warfare to the Region
entries.hint: British Royal Flying Corps and Royal Air Force squadrons conducted extensive aerial reconnaissance and some bombing operations supporting Allenby's advance, the first significant use of powered military aircraft over this specific landscape — a concrete marker of how thoroughly industrial-era warfare technology, developed and refined on European battlefields, had by this point extended its reach even to a theatre many contemporaries still associated primarily with camels, cavalry and ancient biblical geography.
entries.note: Royal Flying Corps and RAF operations supporting the Egyptian Expeditionary Force's Palestine campaign, 1917–1918.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: A chemist's diplomatic campaign in wartime London

entries.label: A Chemist's Diplomatic Campaign in Wartime London
entries.hint: The chemist and Zionist leader Chaim Weizmann built relationships with key British officials during the war years, lobbying persistently for a British declaration of support for Jewish national aspirations in Palestine — his wartime chemistry work reportedly built some personal goodwill with British officials, though historians debate how directly decisive this particular connection was among the many strategic and personal factors that ultimately produced the Balfour Declaration later that same year.
entries.note: Chaim Weizmann's wartime lobbying and relationships with British officials including Arthur Balfour himself; the precise causal weight of any single factor in the Declaration's issuance remains debated among historians rather than fully settled.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: One Ottoman territory becomes contested ground among rival claims

entries.label: One Ottoman Territory Becomes Contested Ground
entries.hint: Within the space of roughly two years, a single Ottoman administrative territory became the subject of three distinct and only partially reconcilable wartime commitments — promised independence to the Arabs, secretly divided between Britain and France, and promised as a Jewish national home — a genuinely unusual concentration of competing great-power and nationalist claims over one piece of ground within so short a span, whose practical resolution through the imposed Mandate system covered in the following folios would shape the region's political geography for the rest of the twentieth century and beyond.
entries.note: Comparative framing of the Hussein-McMahon Correspondence, Sykes-Picot Agreement and Balfour Declaration as three overlapping and only partially compatible wartime commitments, 1915–1917.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: A survivor's voice from a mountain emptied by hunger

entries.label: A Survivor's Voice from the Mountain Famine
entries.hint: Surviving diaries, missionary relief workers' reports and oral histories collected from Mount Lebanon famine survivors describe families reduced to eating grass, bark and animal feed, parents watching children starve while unable to find any food at any price, and entire villages emptied by death and displacement — a level of documented ordinary civilian suffering that, however geographically contained compared to the war's larger battlefronts, ranks among the conflict's most severe humanitarian catastrophes for the population that endured it.
entries.note: Comparative use of surviving contemporary diaries, American and other missionary relief organisations' reports, and later-collected oral histories in reconstructing the 1915–1918 Mount Lebanon famine's lived experience.
